newsitem.title: USA: 'Homecoming' vaults Smith to head House committee.
newsitem.headline: 'Homecoming' vaults Smith to head House committee.

text.p: Bob Smith is returning to Congress in legislative glory, holding more power than he ever expected over Western issues like logging, and assured of becoming a House committee chairman despite a brief retirement.
"It's homecoming for me," Smith, a burly 6-footer from Oregon, said Thursday during a hallway interview punctuated by handshakes and welcome-back greetings from fellow lawmakers.
Republicans were slated on Friday to tab Smith as the new chairman of the House Agriculture Committee, fulfilling a promise made last summer when he agreed to run again.

Capitol Hill experts said no one in recent memory matched the feat of becoming a committee chairman upon re-election after retirement. In most cases lawmakers strive for years to gain control of a committee as the capstone of a career.
When Smith retired in 1994 after 12 years in the House, Republicans were the legislative equivalent of nobodies, forever out-voted. Now Republicans hold the majority and set the agenda.
"Now, they're somebodies. You have to address them as '(Mr) chairman.' It's very different," Smith said.

As Agriculture chairman, Smith planned a busy agenda of looking at Conservation Reserve reforms, examining the impact on U.S. farmers of recent free-trade agreements, whether other nations unfairly block U.S. farm exports "and then I want to take a look at some issues in the West, like what's happening to our (national) forests ... which are slowly disintegrating and burning up because of lack of management."
In coordination with leaders of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Smith said he would file a "forest health" bill.

"We're not going for short-term solutions," Smith said and rebutted environmentalist suspicions that a forest bill would a aimed at more logging. "What we have to do is take care of our forests or lose them."
A buildup of debris and dead trees has made it difficult to control forest fires, he said.

Smith said he also wanted to look at the related issues of the Endangered Species Act, private property rights, and mining and grazing on federal land. There are 191 millon acres of national forests and grasslands.

Smith's influence could be amplified by his request for a seat on the Resources Committee, which also has jurisdiction over federal lands. When he retired Smith was the fifth-ranking Republican on that panel.

Earlier in his career Smith was a cattle rancher and served 22 years in the Oregon Legislature, including four years as speaker of its House of Representatives. While in Congress he opposed what Republicans called the "war on the West" -- efforts to raise grazing fees and limit logging. He also has criticized the impact of bans on logging in large tracts of the Pacific Northwest to protect rare animals.
